newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Excess demand main Irish inflation risk - C.Bank.
newsitem.headline: Excess demand main Irish inflation risk - C.Bank.

text.p: The Central Bank of Ireland said on Thursday that excess demand posed the greatest threat to the country's current low inflation.
"The risk here would be of the demand-pull variety rather than the cost-push variety," the bank's assistant general director, Michael Casey told a news conference.
Casey said the bank could not rule out the risk from international price trends either.
"By policies through the exchange rate and interest rates we would hope to offset any impulse coming from excessive demand," he said at the release of the bank's quarterly bulletin.
The central bank said in its quarterly bulletin that it expected inflation to average 1.75 percent in 1996 but warned that the medium term outlook was less promising.
"Inflation is all relative nowadays," Casey said. "A rate of 1.75 percent might sound good but it is not exceptionally good by European standards."
Casey noted that the EU interim index of consumer prices (IICP), used for intra-European comparisons, was now the more relevant measure.
"Here we rank sixth or seventh in the European class which isn't entirely comfortable," he said.

Irish inflation data, released by the Central Statistics Office earlier on Thursday, showed consumer prices rising 0.5 percent in the three-month period to mid-August and 1.5 percent year-on-year. The IICP rose 0.2 percent on the quarter and 2.2 percent year-on-year.
"We take some credit for the good inflation figure we had this morning and attribute it to the EER (Irish pound's effective exchange rate," Casey said.
He noted that EER had risen by two percent in the first eight months of 1996, providing "a security blanket" for the bank.
Officials said the central bank had to keep a close eye on inflation given the need to meet the Maastricht criteria on European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) in 1997.
"In this situation, where we are on the brink of the biggest economic turning point this century, namely EMU, we can't leave anything to chance. We have to err on the side of caution," Casey said.
Central bank officials said they would like to see credit growth moderating. "We would be in our comfort zone if we got it down to 10 percent," Casey said.

Officials said, however, that the recent rise in money market and retail interest rates had a good signalling effect by showing people that interest rates were not going to continue falling. "It's made people think and that's a good thing," Casey said.
While the money markets triggered the tightening in monetary conditions, Casey said the bank had taken "passive action" by not intervening in the market to keep rates down.
